transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because I can’t really get out from under this feeling that everything that goes wrong is somehow my fault. Like at work, if something slips or there’s a problem, I immediately think it’s because I’m a bad employee, even if I know there are other people and systems involved. And at home too, I keep thinking I’m failing as a homeowner, like I don’t deserve to have what I worked for.

It’s just this constant guilt, like I must have done something wrong or I’m not good enough, and that maybe I deserve to lose everything I’ve built. It’s been really hard to shake, and I think that’s why I finally came in.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in things anymore that used to make you happy, like hobbies or spending time with loved ones?

Yeah… definitely. It’s actually been one of the more upsetting parts, because I can sort of remember being a person who liked things, if that makes sense. I used to be the one planning brunches with friends, like picking the place and making the reservation and getting excited about trying somewhere new. I used to paint in the spare room too — not professionally or anything, just because it felt calming and kind of mine. And I’d go hiking when the weather was nice, or sign up for networking events for work because I liked meeting people and feeling like I was doing something for my future.

Now all of that just feels… flat. Like tasks I’m pretending to care about. I’ll agree to brunch and then spend the whole time feeling like I’m performing being normal. Or I’ll look at my paints and think I should do it because it used to help, but it feels like another chore on a list. Even hiking, which used to make me feel refreshed, just sounds exhausting before I even start. It’s not that I hate those things now, exactly. It’s more like I can’t reach the part of me that used to enjoy them.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… a little over two years now. About two years and one month, if I’m trying to be exact.

I remember at first thinking it was just a rough patch, like maybe I was burned out or stressed and it would lift if I got through a few things. But it didn’t really lift. The sadness and that loss of interest in things have just kind of stayed there, in the background and then sometimes more in the foreground, for all that time. So, yeah… about two years and a month.

Have you ever had periods where your mood was unusually high or you felt much more energetic or restless than usual, where you were doing things more quickly or taking on more than usual — even if it felt good at the time?

I’m… not totally sure how to answer that. I don’t think so, at least not in the way you’re describing, like a clear stretch where I felt unusually high or unstoppable or was taking on a ton of things because I had all this energy.

I mean, I’ve had moments where I get restless, but it feels more like being agitated or unable to settle than feeling good or energized. And sometimes I push myself to get things done because I’m worried I’m falling behind, but it doesn’t feel like I’m suddenly more capable or moving faster in a good way. It’s more like pressure.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed periods like that. If anything, it’s been hard to get myself going.
Have you noticed any periods of time during these two years where your mood was clearly better for a while, even if it eventually got worse again?

Not really in a clean way, no. Like, I can think of little stretches where I was functioning better — getting through work a little more normally, replying to people instead of letting messages sit, maybe agreeing to see someone or run errands without it feeling completely impossible. But even during those times, it wasn’t like I felt actually good or back to myself.

It’s more like the volume got turned down a little bit for a short while, if that makes sense. The low mood and the not caring about things were still there underneath. I’d maybe have a week or a few days where I could fake it better or keep up with things better, and I’d think, okay, maybe I’m coming out of it… but then it would slide back again. And looking back over the whole two years, it feels like that sadness and flatness have been there almost the entire time, just sometimes more manageable and sometimes heavier.
Would you say that your mood has been persistently low or depressed most of the time, nearly every day, over these past two years?

Yes… I would say that. It’s been low most of the time, pretty much nearly every day, for about two years and one month now.

It’s not like every single hour has been exactly the same, but the depression and the loss of interest have just been there with me for that whole stretch. Sometimes it’s a little less intense and I can move through the day better, but it hasn’t really gone away or felt like I was back to normal for any real length of time. So, yes — persistently low is probably the right way to put it.

latest_inference.note: The patient confirmed persistent low mood nearly every day for over two years, with no clear periods of remission and no manic or hypomanic episodes. This rules out recurrent depressive disorder, current episode mild (F33.1) and supports a diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe without psychotic symptoms (F33.2).

inference_history.note: Initial presentation suggests symptoms of depression and anxiety, particularly centered around guilt, self-blame, and worthlessness. This is broad but most consistent with major depressive disorder (moderate to severe) and anxiety disorders, particularly generalized anxiety disorder. No clear psychotic, manic, trauma-related, or obsessive-compulsive features endorsed yet. Further assessment needed to rule in/out comorbid conditions and severity.
